paragraphs: I recently studied abroad at the Chinese University of Hong Kong for two months. Hong Kong has a population about the same as Aichi Prefecture but only two medical schools, so the students are all excellent people. They apparently do not do club activities or part-time jobs either. Also, all higher education in Hong Kong is conducted in English, and medical staff and students are very fluent in English. However, the senior doctors often have a strong Cantonese accent, and my impression was that the younger the person, the more fluent. People in Hong Kong are basically all pro-Japanese, and there were many people, including doctors, who had been to Japan many times. Nurses greeted me with "konnichiwa" in Japanese, and with topics like "I went to Osaka the other day!" and "I know Gundam," I never ran short of things to talk about and could spend my time comfortably.
What differs greatly from Japan in Hong Kong's healthcare system is that Hong Kong is broadly divided into Public Hospitals and Private Hospitals.
Public Hospital: One visit costs only HK$100, and the hospitalization fee is about the same per day, but the waiting time until receiving care is very long.
Private Hospital: These are privately run hospitals, and since there is no government subsidy for the medical costs, the medical expenses patients pay are enormous. But you are seen immediately.
These are the differences. The hospital where I did my clerkship was a Public one, and I was greatly shocked to hear that, for example, for total knee arthroplasty one has to wait about three years.

The official language of Hong Kong is Cantonese, so I could not take histories from patients by myself. However, in the outpatient clinic and on the ward, students and doctors translated the patients' words into English and let me do the physical examination together, and they held rounds and conferences in English, saying "There is an exchange student, so let's do it in English," so they treated me in a very educational way. Throughout the clerkship period, I was able to act relatively freely, joining the discussions of the local students if there were any, or following doctors of the department I was assigned to.

Upper gastrointestinal surgery: I entered the surgical field in almost all operations and was allowed to do relatively simple procedures, which was very educational. As for diseases, my impression was that there are fewer gastric cancer patients than in Japan and relatively more esophageal cancer. Operations using the da Vinci and operations that intentionally resect the stomach in obese patients were also performed. Surgeons also perform upper (esophagus to duodenum) endoscopy, and I could see procedures such as EMR and ESD, which in Japan fall within gastroenterology. As for endoscopy technology, Japan is reportedly more advanced, and several doctors said, "I often go to Japan for training." The doctors were all friendly and harmonious, and it was a department with a very good atmosphere. It is also said to be well regarded by the local students. In particular, Prof. Teoh, who was my supervisor, played Japanese music in the endoscopy room and actively let me do procedures, and treated me very amicably.

Orthopedic surgery: My request before departure had been refused, but when I negotiated directly on site, saying "two months of surgery is long and I want to see other departments too," it was somehow readily accepted. I rotated through the sports team for two weeks and the trauma team for two weeks. Prof. Yung, the professor of the sports team, is a very famous sports orthopedic surgeon who has worked as a sports doctor for 15 years, and many professional athletes came to the professor's outpatient clinic. I was also allowed to do simple physical examinations. In the trauma team I mainly spent time in the operating room. Here too every doctor kindly explained the surgery, and it was very educational.

Prices in Hong Kong are high (especially land prices), and by feel it did not seem very different from Japan. When you hear Hong Kong, you might imagine a city, as typified by the million-dollar night view, but a little outside there are the sea and mountains, and I could enjoy nature through hiking, kayaking and so on. Also, because it is in Asia, badminton is popular, and during my study abroad I dropped in on several adult clubs. I was able to interact with many ordinary citizens regardless of age and gender, and it became a very good memory.

Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude to everyone who supported me, including Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and all the members of the International Collaboration Office, the staff of the Academic Affairs Division, my seniors, my family and the people of the Chinese University of Hong Kong, who gave me this valuable opportunity. And to my roommate 篠田くん, with whom I shared bed and board for two months, thank you very much.
